title: Consistency, CAP and Quorum Arithmetic
subtitle: Stop reciting CAP. Compute what your replication setting actually guarantees.
outcomes: Explain CAP as a statement about partitions, not about everyday operation.
Choose N, W and R for a stated failure tolerance.
Compute the latency and tail-amplification cost of a quorum read.
Give a session guarantee (read-your-writes) without demanding strong consistency everywhere.

blocks.title: The one-sentence version
blocks.t: CAP says: while the network is split, a replica set must either refuse some requests (consistency) or answer with possibly stale data (availability). It says nothing about the 99.99% of the time when the network is healthy — that is what PACELC adds.
1. The model most teams actually need

A distributed data store holds N replicas of each key. A write must be acknowledged by W replicas before it is considered successful. A read contacts R replicas and returns the freshest value it sees. Those three numbers, not the marketing page, define your guarantees.

blocks.caption: What each choice buys and costs
head: Setting
Guarantee
Failure tolerated
Cost
rows: Strong reads, but writes need every replica
No write during any node failure
1 node down for both reads and writes
Eventual; a read may miss the latest write
Fast, but stale reads are visible

blocks.t: The overlap rule is the whole trick. If R + W > N, the read set and the most recent write set must share at least one replica, so at least one node in the read can return the newest value. With N=3, W=2, R=2 the sum is 4: at least one node is in both sets.

blocks.title: Strong on paper, weak in practice
blocks.t: Quorum overlap only gives you strong consistency if the write is applied to those replicas atomically, if read repair or anti-entropy resolves older versions, and if the client reads the maximum version it receives. A sloppy client that returns the first response breaks the guarantee while the configuration still looks correct.
2. Worked example: sizing a quorum
Your product promise: a profile write must never be lost, and the store must keep serving while one node is being patched. Start from the failure tolerance, not from a vendor default.

items: Pick N from the durability requirement. Two copies of a write means losing a node costs nothing; N=3 is the smallest set that tolerates one loss and still has a majority.
Pick W from the write-availability requirement. Tolerating one failure needs W=2 of 3.
Solve R from R+W>N. With N=3 and W=2, R must be at least 2.
Sanity-check read latency: R=2 means the read waits for the slower of two replicas, not for one.
Write down which failure you just gave up. Here: two simultaneous node failures stop writes.

blocks.t: Now change the requirement. If the profile is a public page that may be a few seconds stale, W=2 and R=1 is enough: writes survive a node loss, reads are served by one replica, and the page may show an older name briefly. Same cluster, different API, different guarantee — that is the normal answer. Consistency is a per-operation decision, not a property of the database.
3. The cost you did not budget: tail amplification

A quorum read against 3 replicas takes as long as the second-fastest replica. Fan-out changes the shape of the latency distribution in a way that surprises people: the cluster p99 is not the node p99.

blocks.title: Why p99 becomes p99.8
blocks.t: If each replica independently exceeds x with probability 1%, the chance that at least one of five replicas exceeds x is 1 - 0.99^5 = 4.9%. So the p99 of the fan-out is roughly the per-node p99.8. To promise a cluster p99 you need per-node tails far better than the target.

This is the argument for hedged requests: send to one replica, and after the p95 delay send the same read to a second and take the first answer. Cost: extra load. Benefit: the tail of the fan-out collapses toward the tail of a single replica.
4. Session guarantees: the cheap way to look consistent

Most user-visible staleness is not a database problem — it is a routing problem. A user writes their display name and then reloads the page; the load balancer sends the read to a replica that has not caught up. The database is behaving exactly as configured.

left.title: Read-your-writes, cheaply
items: Route a user's reads to the same replica that took their write, for a short window.
Return the write's logical timestamp and require the read replica to be at least that fresh.
Serve the user their own just-written value from a short-lived client cache.

right.title: Read-your-writes, expensively
items: Send all reads to the primary: simple, and it removes the read scaling you built.
Switch the whole cluster to strong consistency: correct, and it pays coordination on every unrelated read.

blocks.t: Monotonic reads matter too: a user should never see their name change back to an older value as they move between replicas. Sticky routing per session solves both problems at once and is the reason session affinity still exists in front of eventually consistent stores.

blocks.title: Exercise: three APIs, three settings
blocks.prompt: You run one 5-replica store. Choose W and R, and name the guarantee you give up, for: (a) a bank ledger entry, (b) a product catalogue page, (c) a shopping cart that must not lose an item the user just added but may show a stale price.
blocks.hint: Start from the failure you must survive, then from the staleness the user would notice. The cart is the interesting one: it needs read-your-writes, not global strong consistency.
blocks.solution: (a) N=5, W=3, R=3: survives two failures, R+W>N, ledger reads never stale. You give up write availability under three simultaneous failures and pay two round trips. (b) N=5, W=3, R=1: catalogue pages tolerate seconds of staleness; reads are single-replica and cacheable. You give up freshness, not durability. (c) N=5, W=3, R=1 plus a session token: the cart write returns its version, and the user's next read is served by a replica at least that fresh, or from their session cache. You get read-your-writes without strong consistency for everyone else.

blocks.t: 5. Checklist before you claim a consistency model

items: Every read and write path has explicit N, W and R, or an explicit reason to inherit the default.
You can name the failure that stops writes, and whether that is acceptable.
Client libraries return the newest version, not the first response.
Read-your-writes is solved at the session layer for user-facing writes.
You have measured fan-out tail latency, not just per-node latency.
The write path is idempotent, because retries after a timeout are inevitable.

quiz.q: With N=5, W=2 and R=2, what does a read guarantee?
quiz.a: Nothing about freshness
quiz.why: R+W=4 is not greater than N=5, so the read and write sets need not overlap. Writes survive three node failures and reads are cheap, but a read may miss the newest write.

quiz.q: Why does a read against 5 replicas have a worse p99 than a read against 1?
quiz.a: It waits for the slowest of several responses
o: It waits for the slowest of several responses
It uses more CPU per request
It requires a quorum of writes
quiz.why: Fan-out makes the request as slow as the slowest participant, so the cluster tail is the per-node extreme tail — the p99 of the maximum is roughly the per-node p99.8.

quiz.q: A user saves a new avatar and immediately sees the old one. The most likely cause is:
quiz.a: The read hit a replica that had not caught up
o: The read hit a replica that had not caught up
quiz.why: This is the classic read-your-writes gap. The write succeeded; the follow-up read was routed to a lagging replica. Session affinity or a version token fixes it without changing cluster-wide consistency.

quiz.q: Which setting gives the fastest reads while still surviving one node failure for writes?
quiz.why: W=2 of 3 tolerates one failure, and R=1 contacts a single replica. The trade is that reads may be stale, since R+W=3 is not greater than N.

title: Caching in Practice: Hit Ratios, Eviction and Stampedes
subtitle: Decide with arithmetic whether a cache is worth it — and how it will fail.
outcomes: Compute the latency benefit and break-even hit ratio of a cache.
Choose an eviction policy that matches the workload's access pattern.
Pick an invalidation strategy and state its staleness window.
Prevent a cache stampede from turning a cold cache into an outage.

blocks.title: Caches are a bet on locality
blocks.t: A cache only helps if the same data is requested again before it changes. If your access pattern has no reuse, a cache adds a lookup, a copy and an invalidation bug for nothing.
1. Where the cache sits decides what it can fix

head: Layer
Typical hit ratio
What it removes
What it cannot fix
rows: Consistency; it adds a second source of truth

blocks.t: Choose the layer by the cost you are trying to remove. A CDN cannot fix a slow join, and an application cache cannot fix a 400 ms cross-continent round trip.
2. The arithmetic that justifies (or kills) the cache

Let h be the hit ratio, L_cache the cache latency and L_origin the origin latency. Average latency is h·L_cache + (1-h)·L_origin. Set that equal to your target and solve for h to get the break-even ratio.

blocks.title: Worked: 90/10 at 2 ms and 120 ms
blocks.t: 0.9 × 2 + 0.1 × 120 = 13.8 ms, against 120 ms uncached — an 8.7× improvement. Break-even for a 20 ms target: h × 2 + (1-h) × 120 < 20 gives h > 84.7%. Below that hit ratio the cache is not buying you the latency you promised.

Capacity follows the same logic. Suppose the table is 40 GB, and 20% of rows serve 80% of requests. An 8 GB cache can hold that hot set; the expected hit ratio is near 80%, not 100%, because the remaining 20% of requests touch cold rows that will always miss. Size for the working set, not for the table.
3. Read and write patterns

head: Pattern
How it works
Staleness window
Use when
rows: App reads cache, on miss reads origin and populates
Cache library loads from origin on miss
You want the logic in one place
Write to cache and origin together
None, if the write is atomic
Reads must never see old data
Write to cache, flush to origin later

blocks.title: The two hard problems, restated
blocks.t: Invalidation is hard because the cache does not know why the data changed. A write path that forgets one of five update routes leaves a stale entry until TTL. Versioned keys (user:42:v7) make invalidation a pointer swap, at the cost of garbage you must collect.
4. Eviction: pick for the access pattern, not by habit

left.title: Good fits
items: LRU: recency-dominated traffic such as sessions and feeds.
LFU: stable popularity, where a one-off scan should not evict hot keys.
TTL-only: data with a natural lifetime, such as tokens or price quotes.
Allowlist: never cache the paths that must always be correct (balances, permissions).

right.title: Common mistakes
items: LRU in front of a nightly full scan: the scan evicts everything useful.
Unbounded cache: it becomes a memory leak with a hit ratio.
No metric on evictions: you cannot tell 'too small' from 'wrong policy'.
Caching authorisation decisions with no invalidation on role change.

blocks.t: Belady's optimal policy — evict the item whose next use is furthest away — is not implementable online, but it is the right benchmark. If your measured hit ratio is close to Belady's for a trace, your policy is fine and the cache is simply too small.
5. Stampedes, and the math that prevents them

Ten thousand requests per second hit a key with a 60-second TTL. If the key expires everywhere at once, all 10,000 requests miss in the same instant and the origin receives 10,000 queries for one row. It was handling 167 per second.

items: Jitter the TTL: store ttl = base + random(0, base × 0.2). Expiries spread across a 12-second window, cutting the burst by an order of magnitude.
Coalesce misses: the first request takes a per-key lock and recomputes; the rest wait briefly and read the fresh value.
Serve stale while revalidating: return the expired value immediately and refresh in the background. Staleness is bounded by the refresh time, not the TTL.
Add a negative cache for missing keys, with a short TTL, so a request for a nonexistent id does not hammer the origin.
Warm the cache after deploys and before known traffic spikes, rather than letting the first users warm it.

blocks.title: Exercise: is the cache worth it?
blocks.prompt: Origin latency is 200 ms p50, cache lookup is 5 ms. Product wants p50 under 50 ms. Your measured hit ratio is 78%. Does the cache meet the target, and what would you change?
blocks.hint: Compute the average, then the break-even hit ratio for the target.
blocks.solution: Average = 0.78 × 5 + 0.22 × 200 = 3.9 + 44 = 47.9 ms, so it just meets the target. Break-even for 50 ms: 5h + 200(1-h) < 50 gives h > 76.9%. At 78% you have almost no margin — one traffic shift defeats the promise. Options: raise the hit ratio with a larger cache or better key design, cut origin latency for misses, or use stale-while-revalidate so misses are cheap instead of slow.

blocks.t: 6. Operating a cache

items: Hit ratio, evictions and miss latency are on a dashboard, per key family.
Every cached entity has a stated maximum staleness.
Writes invalidate through one code path, not five.
Keys are versioned or namespaced so a schema change cannot serve old shapes.
A cold cache is tested: can the origin survive 100% miss traffic?
Sensitive data is not cached in shared layers without per-user keying.

quiz.q: Cache hit ratio is 80%, cache latency 2 ms, origin 120 ms. Average latency is:
quiz.why: 0.8 × 2 + 0.2 × 120 = 1.6 + 24 = 25.6 ms. The miss path dominates because misses are 20% of traffic paying 120 ms.

quiz.q: Why does adding random jitter to TTLs reduce origin load?
quiz.a: It spreads expiries so keys do not miss simultaneously
o: It spreads expiries so keys do not miss simultaneously
It increases the hit ratio directly
It removes the need for invalidation
quiz.why: Synchronised expiry turns a steady miss rate into a burst. Jitter flattens the burst back into the steady rate the origin was sized for.

quiz.q: A nightly job scans the whole table through a cache using LRU. The likely result is:
quiz.a: Hot keys are evicted and the hit ratio collapses
o: Hot keys are evicted and the hit ratio collapses
The scan gets faster and nothing else changes
quiz.why: A full scan touches every key once, and LRU treats each as the most recent. Useful hot entries are pushed out, so the next real traffic misses. LFU or a separate cache for scans avoids this.

quiz.q: Which data should be allowlisted out of the cache entirely?
quiz.a: Balances and permission checks
quiz.why: Some reads must always be correct or must reflect a change immediately. Caching them turns every invalidation bug into a financial or security incident.

title: Resilience Patterns That Actually Hold
subtitle: Timeouts, retries, breakers and bulkheads, sized with numbers instead of hope.
outcomes: Derive per-call timeouts from an endpoint SLO.
Compute retry amplification and bound it.
Implement a circuit breaker with explicit states and thresholds.
Isolate dependencies with bulkheads and degrade deliberately.

blocks.title: The goal is not zero failures
blocks.t: It is a bounded, predictable failure. A service that returns a stale answer in 30 ms is healthy under stress; one that holds 2,000 threads waiting 30 seconds is down, and it takes its callers with it.
1. Timeouts come from a budget, not from a default

Write the endpoint's latency budget first, then divide it. A product page has a 800 ms p99 target. The handler needs 100 ms for its own work, and calls three dependencies sequentially: recommendations, inventory, pricing.

head: Step
Budget
Rule
rows: Hard dependency: fail the page if exceeded
Soft dependency: on timeout, render without it
Absorbs GC, network jitter, TLS handshakes

blocks.t: Two design rules fall out of the table. First, a timeout longer than the caller's remaining budget is wasted waiting: the caller has already given up, so the callee is doing work nobody will read. Second, soft dependencies should time out earlier and degrade, not fail the request.
2. Retries multiply load — compute by how much
If a call fails with probability p and you attempt it A times, the expected number of calls per logical request is (1 - p^A) / (1 - p). That is your load multiplier against a failing dependency.

blocks.title: Three layers of retries is 27 calls
blocks.t: If the gateway retries 3 times, the service retries 3 times, and the client retries 3 times, one user action can become 27 backend calls — precisely when the backend is already failing. Retry at one layer only, and make that layer's budget global.
Retries also require idempotency. A timeout does not mean the write failed; it means you do not know. Without an idempotency key, the retry creates a second order.
3. Backoff with jitter, in code
Note what the code refuses to do: retry non-retryable errors, retry forever, or retry without a cap. A retry loop that ignores those three rules is a self-inflicted denial of service.
4. Circuit breakers: fail fast, recover carefully

nodes.label: Closed
nodes.sub: calls flow; count failures in a rolling window

nodes.label: Open
nodes.sub: fail immediately for a cooldown; no calls leave

blocks.t: Thresholds matter more than the pattern. A breaker that opens after 3 failures out of 10 will flap on normal noise. Use a ratio over a minimum sample: open when error rate exceeds 50% with at least 20 requests in 30 seconds, cool down for 10 seconds, then allow 3 trial requests.

blocks.title: Breakers protect the caller, not the callee
blocks.t: The point is to stop your threads, connections and memory being consumed by calls that cannot succeed. It does nothing for the failing service — that needs load shedding and backpressure on its side.
5. Bulkheads: bound the blast radius

A service pool of 100 database connections shared by three features is one pool with three ways to die. Give each feature its own slice: 60 for the interactive path, 25 for background jobs, 15 for admin tools. When the nightly job saturates its 25, users still have 60.

The same idea applies to thread pools per dependency, separate queues per tenant, and separate clusters per customer tier. You are choosing who gets hurt first, deliberately, instead of letting arrival order decide.
6. Degrade on purpose

head: Dependency fails
Bad response
Good response
rows: Fail the page: wrong money is worse than no page

blocks.t: Write this table down before the incident. Deciding under pressure which data may be stale is how teams ship a financial bug.

blocks.title: Exercise: size the defences
blocks.prompt: Your API calls a payments provider. p99 is 1.2 s, the endpoint SLA is 2 s, and the provider has had two 20-minute outages this quarter. Design timeout, retry, breaker and fallback.
blocks.hint: Ask what a duplicate charge costs versus a failed checkout, and what the user should see during an outage.
blocks.solution: Timeout 1.5 s (inside the 2 s budget, above the provider p99 so normal traffic completes). One retry, only for timeouts and 5xx, with an idempotency key so a duplicate cannot charge twice — effective failure rate falls from ~1% to ~0.01% while load rises ~1.01×. Breaker: open at 50% errors over 20 requests in 30 s, 10 s cooldown, 3 half-open trials. Fallback: queue the payment attempt and show 'processing', never a fake success — a wrong charge is worse than a delayed one. Alert on open breaker, not just on errors.

blocks.t: 7. Review checklist

items: Every outgoing call has an explicit timeout below the caller's remaining budget.
Retries happen at one layer, with a cap, jitter, and idempotency.
Breakers use a ratio with a minimum sample, not a raw failure count.
Connection and thread pools are partitioned by feature or tenant.
Each soft dependency has a written degraded mode.
Dashboards show open breakers, retry rate and pool saturation.

quiz.q: The endpoint budget is 500 ms and the callee's timeout is 2 s. The problem is:
quiz.a: The caller gives up long before the callee stops working
o: The caller gives up long before the callee stops working
The timeout is too short to be safe
The callee will retry too often
quiz.why: A timeout longer than the caller's remaining budget wastes the callee's capacity on responses nobody will read. Timeouts should shrink as they go down the call chain.

quiz.q: At 50% failure, 5 attempts give roughly what load multiplier?
quiz.why: (1 - 0.5^5)/(1 - 0.5) = (1 - 0.03125)/0.5 = 1.94. Retries roughly double the load on an already failing dependency while cutting the user-visible failure rate to about 3%.

quiz.q: A circuit breaker primarily protects:
quiz.a: The caller's resources
quiz.why: It stops the caller from spending threads, connections and memory on calls that cannot succeed. The failing service needs its own shedding and backpressure.

quiz.q: Retrying a payment timeout without an idempotency key risks:
quiz.a: Charging the customer twice
quiz.why: A timeout means unknown outcome, not failure. The original request may have succeeded; the retry creates a second charge unless the provider can deduplicate by key.

title: CQRS and Event Sourcing, End to End
subtitle: One write model, many read models, and a log you can replay after a bug.
outcomes: Separate a write model from read models and state the consistency gap between them.
Append events with optimistic concurrency instead of overwriting state.
Build an idempotent projection with a checkpoint.
Replay or rebuild a projection after a defect, without touching the write side.
Decide when CQRS and event sourcing are the wrong choice.

blocks.title: Two separate ideas
blocks.t: CQRS is about separating the write path from the read path. Event sourcing is about storing changes as the source of truth. You can adopt either alone. Most teams that regret event sourcing adopted both at once, for a domain that only needed one.
1. The problem CQRS solves

An order service must answer two very different questions. Writes: accept an order, reserve stock, apply a discount — they need transactions, invariants and current state. Reads: order history, spend by month, fulfilment queue — they need denormalised shapes, indexes and heavy filtering.

One table cannot be optimal for both. Add an index for the read and writes slow down; add a lock for the write and reads queue behind it. CQRS accepts the duplication: a normalised write model and one or more purpose-built read models fed by events.

blocks.title: The gap is now your API's problem
blocks.t: Right after a write succeeds, the projection may not have it yet. Either the API returns the new version and the client waits for it, or the UI reads the write model for its own recent changes. Ignoring this produces 'I placed the order and it is not in my history' bug reports.
2. Appending events with optimistic concurrency
State is derived; the log is the truth. Every aggregate carries a version, and an append only succeeds if the version you read is still the version on disk. That single constraint replaces row locks.

CREATE TABLE order_events (
  order_id     UUID        NOT NULL,
  version      INT         NOT NULL,
  event_type   TEXT        NOT NULL,
  payload      JSONB       NOT NULL,
  recorded_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, version)          -- the concurrency check
);

-- Append only if this is the next version. 0 rows affected = someone else won.
INSERT INTO order_events (order_id, version, event_type, payload)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'OrderPlaced', $3);

Two concurrent writers both read version 7 and both try to insert version 8. The primary key rejects the second, the service retries by re-reading, and no lost update is possible. No SELECT FOR UPDATE, no distributed lock, and the same mechanism works across regions.
Load state by folding the events. With a few hundred events per aggregate this is trivial; beyond that, snapshot every N events and fold from the snapshot.
3. A projection that can be rebuilt

-- Projection state + its own checkpoint, in the same database.
CREATE TABLE order_history (
  order_id    UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id UUID NOT NULL,
  total_cents BIGINT NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,
  placed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE projection_checkpoint (
  name       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  position   BIGINT NOT NULL
);

-- The consumer loop, in words:
-- 1. read events with position > checkpoint, ordered
-- 2. apply each one with an idempotent upsert
-- 3. advance the checkpoint in the SAME transaction as the upsert

Step 3 is the part people skip. If the projection write commits but the checkpoint does not, the event is replayed — so the upsert must be idempotent. If the checkpoint commits but the write does not, the event is silently lost. One transaction, both writes.
4. Replay is the payoff — and the trap
A discount calculation was wrong for three weeks. With event sourcing, you fix the handler and replay the log from the beginning into a new projection. No data repair script, no lost history.

left.title: Replay, done safely
items: Build the new projection beside the old one, not over it.
Compare row counts and a few known totals before switching reads.
Throttle the consumer so replay does not starve live traffic.
Keep the old projection until the new one has served traffic for a day.

right.title: Replay, done dangerously
items: Truncating the live table and replaying in place: no rollback.
Replaying while consumers are still writing to the same target.
Assuming events are immutable while a migration rewrites them in place.
Forgetting that external side effects (emails, payments) were already sent.

blocks.t: That last point is important: replay re-derives state, it does not re-send email. Side effects belong in a separate, non-replayed consumer with its own deduplication.
5. Evolving events without breaking history
Events are a contract with your past. You cannot edit an old event to match new code. Add fields with defaults, keep old event types readable, and upcast on read.

items: Additive change: a new optional field with a documented default. Old events still parse.
Semantic change: introduce a new event type (OrderPlacedV2) and teach handlers both.
Removal: stop writing a field, keep reading it, and only delete after every aggregate's history is outside the retention you care about.
Upcasting: a translation layer at read time, tested against real historical payloads.

blocks.t: 6. When not to use this

items: You need a simple CRUD admin screen: a table is cheaper and clearer.
Nobody will ever ask 'how did this get into this state?' — the audit value is the main justification.
Your team has no operational experience with consumers, offsets and replays.
You cannot accept eventual consistency between write and read.
Event volume is enormous and projections would be the bottleneck anyway.

blocks.title: Exercise: design the read side
blocks.prompt: An order service emits OrderPlaced, OrderPaid, OrderShipped, OrderRefunded. Product wants (a) a customer order history page, (b) daily revenue by country, (c) a warehouse pick list of paid, unshipped orders. Design the projections and say what happens on replay.
blocks.hint: One projection per access pattern. Think about what each needs to be keyed by and whether it is a full rebuild or an increment.
blocks.solution: (a) order_history keyed by order_id, with customer_id indexed, updated by all four events. (b) revenue_daily keyed by (day, country), incremented on OrderPaid and decremented on OrderRefunded — an idempotent increment needs the event position stored per key, or recompute from a dedupe table. (c) pick_list keyed by order_id, inserted on OrderPaid, deleted on OrderShipped. On replay: all three rebuild from position zero; (b) must be recomputed rather than incremented blindly, or increments must be deduplicated by event id. Verify (b) against an independent SUM over order_events before switching.

blocks.t: 7. Review checklist

items: The write model's invariants are enforced in one place.
Every append is version-checked; retries re-read first.
Each projection has a checkpoint committed atomically with its writes.
Query handlers tolerate being a few seconds behind.
Replay has been run once, in staging, with a measurement.
Side effects are outside the replayable path.

quiz.q: What enforces 'no lost updates' in an event-sourced aggregate?
quiz.a: A unique constraint on (aggregate_id, version)
o: A read lock on the table
quiz.why: The append is rejected if the version already exists, so a concurrent writer must re-read and retry. It works the same way in one region or five.

quiz.q: Why must the projection checkpoint commit with the projection write?
quiz.a: Otherwise an event is either lost or applied twice
o: Otherwise an event is either lost or applied twice
To avoid needing a primary key
quiz.why: Separate commits create a gap: write-then-crash loses the checkpoint, checkpoint-then-crash loses the write. One transaction makes the pair atomic, and idempotent upserts handle redelivery.

quiz.q: Replaying a projection re-sends welcome emails unless:
quiz.a: Side effects are handled by a separate, deduplicated consumer
o: Side effects are handled by a separate, deduplicated consumer
quiz.why: Replay re-derives state only. Anything that already left the system — email, payment, webhook — must live outside the replay path or be deduplicated by event id.

quiz.q: Which is a sign CQRS is the wrong tool?
quiz.a: An admin CRUD screen with no read/write contention
o: An admin CRUD screen with no read/write contention
A dashboard needing five denormalised views
A domain requiring a full audit trail
quiz.why: CQRS pays for itself by resolving contention or enabling different read shapes. On a simple CRUD screen it adds a second model, a lag and a class of bugs for no benefit.

title: From Domain Model to Service Schema
subtitle: Constraints, indexes, tenancy and migrations — the parts that are expensive to change later.
outcomes: Turn entities and relationships into tables with enforced invariants.
Choose indexes from the queries, including composite, partial and covering ones.
Isolate tenants with a column plus row-level security, not with application discipline.
Ship a breaking schema change as three backward-compatible deploys.

blocks.title: The schema is the only invariant that cannot be bypassed
blocks.t: Every application bug, every script, every future service and every analyst goes through the same tables. A constraint written once holds forever; a validation rule written in one service is enforced until someone writes the second service.
1. Model first, then DDL

Start from the nouns and the rules, not from a table list. For a course platform: a customer places orders; an order contains line items; each line item references a product; an order has a status that only moves forward.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id    UUID        NOT NULL,
  customer_id  UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  status       TEXT        NOT NULL
               CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','cancelled')),
  total_cents  BIGINT      NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  placed_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  shipped_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  CONSTRAINT shipped_needs_date
    CHECK (status <> 'shipped' OR shipped_at IS NOT NULL)
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id     UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  line_no      INT  NOT NULL,
  product_id   UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity     INT  NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_cents   BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (unit_cents >= 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no)
);

Three rules are now guaranteed regardless of client: status is one of four values, a shipped order has a delivery date, and no line has a non-positive quantity. Each of those is a bug class you will never debug.

blocks.title: Constraints have a cost
blocks.t: Every CHECK and foreign key is work on the write path, and a foreign key takes a shared lock on the referenced row. At very high write rates, teams move checks into the application deliberately — and then must accept that a bug becomes corrupt data. Make that trade explicitly.
2. Indexes come from queries, not from columns
Write the five queries that matter, then index for them. For 'recent paid orders for a customer', the index is (tenant_id, customer_id, placed_at DESC) with a partial predicate on status.

-- Partial + composite: only rows the query needs, in the query's order.
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_recent
  ON orders (tenant_id, customer_id, placed_at DESC)
  WHERE status = 'paid';

-- Covering: the query never touches the table.
CREATE INDEX order_items_by_product
  ON order_items (product_id) INCLUDE (quantity, unit_cents);

Column order is not cosmetic. A composite index is usable from its leftmost column: (tenant_id, customer_id) serves a query filtering on tenant alone, but (customer_id, tenant_id) does not. Put equality columns first, then the range or sort column.

Then read the plan. If EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a sequential scan on a large table, either the index does not match the predicate or the planner decided the predicate is not selective enough — and adding another index will not change that.
3. Tenancy: make the leak impossible

A tenant_id column plus a WHERE clause in every query works until one query forgets it. Row-level security moves the check into the database, where a forgotten clause returns nothing instead of someone else's data.

Two operational notes. The setting must be set per transaction, not once per pooled connection, or a reused connection inherits the previous tenant. And policies should be tested with an automated cross-tenant read that must return zero rows.
4. Migrations as three deploys
Renaming a column is a breaking change if old code and new code ever run at the same time — which they always do during a rolling deploy. Expand/contract removes the breakage.

items: Expand: add the new column or table, nullable, with a backfill job. Old code ignores it; new code writes to both.
Migrate: deploy code that reads the new column and still writes both. Verify the backfill is complete and monitors are clean.
Contract: deploy code that only knows the new column, then drop the old one in a later migration.

blocks.title: Never mix DDL and data backfill in one transaction
blocks.t: A long backfill holds locks and blocks writes. Add the column, commit, backfill in batches with a throttle, then add the NOT NULL and the index concurrently.

blocks.title: Exercise: design the matchmaking queue table
blocks.prompt: A game needs a queue of waiting players: skill rating, region, party size, enqueue time. Matches pull 10 players from one region within a rating band. Design the table and the index that makes the pull cheap, then say what happens at 50k queued players.
blocks.hint: Equality first (region), then range (rating), and think about how rows leave the table.
blocks.solution: Table queue_entries(id, player_id, party_id, region, rating, party_size, enqueued_at, expires_at), unique on player_id so a player cannot double-queue, check on party_size. Index (region, rating, enqueued_at) so the matcher scans a narrow band per region. Rows are deleted on match, so the table stays proportional to queue depth, not history. At 50k queued, the matcher should not scan: it seeks to a rating band, reads ~100 candidates, and expands the band over time; expired rows are removed by TTL or a sweeper, and regional sharding keeps each matcher's working set small.

blocks.t: 5. Review checklist

items: Every invariant has a constraint or a documented reason it cannot.
Each index maps to a named query; unused indexes are removed.
Tenant isolation is enforced below the application and tested cross-tenant.
Schema changes are expand/contract, with the backfill throttled.
Plans are reviewed for the top queries after every schema change.

quiz.q: Which index serves WHERE tenant_id = ? AND customer_id = ? ORDER BY placed_at DESC?
quiz.a: (tenant_id, customer_id, placed_at DESC)
quiz.why: Equality columns first in any order, then the sort column. The leftmost-prefix rule makes the other orderings unusable for this predicate.

quiz.q: Row-level security helps mainly because:
quiz.a: A forgotten WHERE clause returns nothing instead of another tenant's rows
o: A forgotten WHERE clause returns nothing instead of another tenant's rows
It removes the need for indexes
quiz.why: The policy is applied by the database to every query, including ad-hoc and future services. It converts a data breach into a bug report.

quiz.q: In expand/contract, why add the new column as nullable first?
quiz.a: Old code is still running during the rolling deploy
o: Old code is still running during the rolling deploy
quiz.why: A NOT NULL column with no default breaks inserts from the old version still serving traffic. Expand, backfill, switch reads, then enforce and contract.

quiz.q: A partial index on WHERE status = 'paid' is useful because:
quiz.a: It only indexes the rows that queries actually filter on
o: It only indexes the rows that queries actually filter on
quiz.why: Smaller index, less write amplification, faster scans — but only for queries whose predicate matches the index's WHERE clause.

title: Disaster Recovery: Turning an Availability Promise into a Plan
subtitle: RPO, RTO, backup sizing and the drill that proves any of it works.
outcomes: Distinguish high availability from disaster recovery.
Derive backup frequency from an RPO and a restore strategy from an RTO.
Size backup storage and restore time with real arithmetic.
Write a runbook that another engineer can execute at 3 a.m.

blocks.title: HA is not DR
blocks.t: High availability keeps serving when a node dies. Disaster recovery restores service when the whole cluster, region or data set is gone — including the case where the data itself was corrupted an hour ago and replicated everywhere.
1. Start from two numbers

head: Term
Question it answers
Drives
rows: How much data may we lose?
Backup frequency, replication mode, WAL retention
How long may we be down?
Warm standby vs pilot light vs restore-from-backup

blocks.t: A 99.95% availability target allows about 21.6 minutes of downtime per month. If your RTO is 4 hours, you cannot meet that target with a restore-from-backup strategy alone — you need a standby that can take over in minutes.

blocks.title: Worked: backup interval vs RPO
blocks.t: Full backups nightly and no continuous log means an RPO of up to 24 hours: a failure at 23:59 loses a day. Continuous change capture into object storage every 5 minutes gives an RPO of 5 minutes, at the cost of storage and a restore that must replay those increments.
2. Restore time is arithmetic, not optimism

Suppose the database is 2 TB and the restore path sustains 100 MB/s from object storage. That is 2,000,000 MB / 100 MB/s = 20,000 seconds, or about 5.5 hours — before replaying increments and rebuilding indexes.

items: Measure the actual restore throughput, not the vendor's peak.
Add replay time for the incremental log up to the failure point.
Add index rebuild and verification time.
Add DNS/connection cutover and cache warmup.
Compare with the RTO. If it does not fit, change the strategy instead of the slide.

blocks.t: 3. Store backups where the failure cannot reach them

A backup in the same region, on the same account, with the same credentials is not a backup — it is a copy that shares the blast radius. Use a separate account or project, a separate region, immutable retention, and credentials that the production cluster cannot delete.

blocks.title: The ransomware and fat-finger cases
blocks.t: Point-in-time recovery is what saves you when an operator or an attacker deletes the data and the deletion replicates. Retention must be longer than your detection time. Thirty days is a common floor for business data; seven days is usually too short to notice a silent corruption.
4. Verify, don't assume
Restore verification has three levels, and most teams only do the first.

items: The backup job reports success.
A restore of a sample table completes into a scratch environment.
A full restore is timed against the RTO, quarterly, with the on-call engineer driving.
Row counts and checksums are compared against the source before cutover.
The runbook was followed by someone who did not write it.

blocks.t: 5. The runbook, in the order you will need it

items: Declare the incident and name one decision-maker. Ambiguous authority doubles the outage.
Stop the damage: revoke credentials, stop the job, isolate the cluster.
Choose the restore point. Ask what the last known-good state was, not what the latest backup is.
Restore into a new environment, never over the damaged one.
Validate with business queries: counts, totals, a few recent records.
Cut over, then watch error rate and latency for twice as long as you think you need.
Write the timeline while it is fresh; the postmortem is the only part that prevents the repeat.

blocks.title: Exercise: pick a strategy
blocks.prompt: A B2B SaaS has a 4-hour RTO, a 15-minute RPO, a 3 TB database and a restore rate of 150 MB/s. Their contract fines 10% of monthly fees per hour of downtime. What do you recommend, and what does it cost versus a warm standby?
blocks.hint: Compute restore time first; then decide whether the fine and the engineering cost justify a standby.
blocks.solution: Restore alone is 3,000,000 MB / 150 MB/s ≈ 5.5 hours, so restore-from-backup misses the 4-hour RTO before increments and index rebuilds. Options: raise restore throughput with parallel download and pre-built indexes (may reach ~3 hours), or run a warm standby in a second region with continuous replication: RTO minutes, RPO seconds, at roughly double compute plus cross-region egress. Given the contractual fine, the standby pays for itself on the first incident; keep nightly logical backups off-site as the corruption escape hatch, because replication faithfully copies corruption.

blocks.t: 6. What to show in review

items: RPO and RTO are written down and owned by a named person.
Backup frequency and retention follow from those numbers.
Backups live in a separate account and region, with immutable retention.
The last restore drill has a date, a duration and a person.
There is a documented decision on what data is allowed to be lost.

quiz.a: 5.5 hours
quiz.why: 3 TB ≈ 3,000,000 MB; divided by 150 MB/s gives ~20,000 s, or 5.5 hours — before replaying increments and rebuilding indexes.

quiz.a: Corruption or deletion that replicates to the standby
o: Corruption or deletion that replicates to the standby
quiz.why: Replication copies whatever happens, including a bad migration or a deletion. Only point-in-time recovery with retention beyond your detection window lets you go back before the damage.

quiz.q: RPO primarily determines:
quiz.a: How often changes must be captured
o: How often changes must be captured
quiz.why: RPO is acceptable data loss, so it sets capture frequency (and replication mode). RTO sets the recovery mechanism and its speed.

quiz.q: The safest place to stop a cascading outage is:
quiz.a: Early, by revoking access and isolating the failing component
o: Early, by revoking access and isolating the failing component
By restarting every service at once
By restoring from the latest backup immediately
quiz.why: Damage control comes before diagnosis. Restoring before you know what was corrupted risks re-introducing the fault and destroying evidence.

title: Netcode: Ticks, Prediction and the Latency Budget
subtitle: How a 100 ms round trip becomes a playable game, with the numbers behind it.
outcomes: Trace input, simulation, broadcast and correction through a tick loop.
Choose a tick rate and compute the resulting input delay.
Explain what the client may predict safely and what it may not.
Estimate bandwidth per player and decide what needs interest management.

blocks.title: The constraint is physics plus trust
blocks.t: Light takes about 67 ms to cross the Atlantic in fibre. No architecture removes that. Netcode exists to hide the round trip from the player without handing authority to the client, because the client is the adversary.
1. The loop

Every input is numbered. The server acknowledges the last input it applied. The client keeps unacknowledged inputs so it can replay them after a correction. That sequence number is the spine of the whole design.
2. Tick rate, and what it really costs

head: Tick rate
Tick length
Suits
Cost
rows: Cheap; visible latency in action games
Very expensive; marginal for remote play

blocks.t: Doubling the tick rate doubles simulation cost and roughly doubles snapshot production. It does not halve the player's round trip. Beyond about 60 Hz the visible benefit is mostly hit registration, which is why competitive shooters pay for it and co-op games do not.
3. The latency budget, itemised

Take a 100 ms RTT player on a 30 Hz server. One-way trip is 50 ms. The input waits for the next tick (up to 33 ms), the server simulates (say 2 ms), and the snapshot travels back (50 ms). That is up to 135 ms before the player sees their own action — enough to feel wrong.
Client-side prediction removes the two network legs for the local player: the client applies the input immediately and shows the result. What remains is correction when the server disagrees.

left.title: Safe to predict
items: Your own movement, animation and camera.
Weapon fire effects and local audio.
UI acknowledgement of an action.

right.title: Never predict authoritatively
items: Damage dealt to another player.
Loot, currency or inventory changes.
Match outcome, scoring, or rank.
Anything the server must be able to reject.

blocks.title: Prediction is a loan against reconciliation
blocks.t: Every predicted action must be correctable. If a prediction can produce an effect that cannot be undone — a purchase, a kill, a rank change — do not predict it. Show a pending state instead.
4. Reconciliation without visible snapping

The server sends the authoritative state plus the last input it processed. The client compares that state with its own record of that tick, drops acknowledged inputs, replays the remainder, and blends the visual difference over a few frames.
The blend is not cosmetic. A hard snap of 40 cm is read by players as a bug or as cheating; the same correction spread over 100 ms is read as normal movement.
5. Other players are interpolated, not predicted

You cannot know another player's next input, so their movement is rendered slightly in the past — typically 100 ms behind the newest snapshot — and interpolated between the two most recent states. This trades a little accuracy for smooth motion despite jitter and packet loss.

Extrapolation is the alternative: predict where they are going. It looks better on a clean network and much worse when someone stops, turns, or lags. Most games interpolate; a few extrapolate with a short cap.
6. Bandwidth: do the multiplication before the design review

Sixty-four players, 20 snapshots per second, 60 bytes of state per player: 64 × 20 × 60 = 76,800 bytes per second per client, about 77 KB/s down — 0.6 Mbit/s. That is fine. Now make it 200 players in an open world: 240 KB/s per client, and the server is producing 200 × 200 × 20 × 60 bytes ≈ 48 MB/s of egress.

items: Interest management: only send entities within a radius or in the same room. This is the single biggest win.
Delta compression: send changed fields against the last acknowledged snapshot.
Quantisation: positions as 16-bit fixed point instead of 32-bit floats.
Priority: update nearby combatants every tick, distant ones every few ticks.
Reliability split: state on unreliable datagrams, events (chat, purchases) on a reliable channel.

blocks.title: TCP is usually the wrong transport for state
blocks.t: Head-of-line blocking means one lost packet stalls every later packet, including fresher state that supersedes it. Games send state over UDP with their own sequencing, and use reliable channels only for events that must not be lost.

blocks.title: Exercise: budget a 40-player shooter
blocks.prompt: 40 players, 30 Hz, 48 bytes per player snapshot. Compute per-client downstream bandwidth. Then decide what to do for a player with 2% packet loss and 180 ms RTT.
blocks.hint: Multiply players × rate × bytes. For the bad connection, think about what to drop first and what must remain authoritative.
blocks.solution: 40 × 30 × 48 = 57,600 B/s ≈ 58 KB/s down per client, ~0.46 Mbit/s — comfortable. For the 180 ms / 2% player: keep authority on the server, increase interpolation delay to ~200 ms so two snapshots usually arrive in time, send redundant recent snapshots so a lost packet is covered by the next, reduce their update rate for distant entities, and never let them predict damage. If they still cannot keep up, degrade their view (fewer entities) rather than their correctness.

blocks.t: 7. Review checklist

items: Every input is sequenced and acknowledged.
Each predicted action is reversible or purely cosmetic.
Corrections are blended, never snapped.
Remote players are interpolated with a stated delay.
Bandwidth is computed, not estimated, at target player count.
Interest management exists before the world grows.

quiz.q: Why does the client keep unacknowledged inputs?
quiz.a: To replay them after a server correction
o: To replay them after a server correction
quiz.why: The server's snapshot reflects only inputs it has processed. The client rewinds to that state and reapplies pending inputs, so the local view stays consistent and responsive.

quiz.q: A 30 Hz server adds up to how much delay before simulating a new input?
quiz.a: 33 ms
quiz.why: Inputs are processed on ticks; worst case is one full tick period, 1/30 s ≈ 33 ms. Higher tick rates shrink this, at higher CPU cost.

quiz.q: Which should never be client-predicted as final?
quiz.a: Damage dealt to another player
quiz.why: Predicted damage can be rejected by the server, producing a visible lie and an exploit path. Predict only what you can undo.

quiz.q: Interest management mainly reduces:
quiz.a: Per-client bandwidth and server egress
quiz.why: Sending only nearby entities cuts both the snapshot size and the fan-out. It scales better than any compression tweak.

title: Matchmaking by Design
subtitle: Tickets, pools, quality functions and the queue-time trade you cannot avoid.
outcomes: Trace a ticket from submission to assigned game server.
Design pool expansion that trades match quality for queue time deliberately.
Write a match function with an explicit quality metric.
Size the matcher from queue depth and arrival rate.

blocks.title: Matchmaking is a search with a deadline
blocks.t: Perfect matches exist in theory and never in your queue. Every design decision is about how fast to widen the search before the player leaves.
1. The pipeline

The ticket carries what the matcher needs: player id, skill rating, region, party size, mode, and enqueue time. The pool is the set of tickets eligible to be matched together. The profile declares the match shape — 5v5, one region, rating band. The match function is the only custom code, and it returns proposed matches with a quality score.

blocks.title: Separate matchmaking from server allocation
blocks.t: Finding ten compatible players and finding a machine to host them are different problems with different failure modes. Keep the match function pure: given tickets and a profile, propose matches. Let the Director handle allocation, retries and player connection details.
2. The unavoidable trade
Queue time and match quality pull in opposite directions. Tighten the rating band and the queue gets longer; widen it and stomp rates rise. You cannot escape this, so make it explicit and measurable.

head: Queue age
Rating band
Region set
Expected effect
rows: Match now or lose the player

blocks.title: Never widen latency to save skill
blocks.t: A 200 ms match is not a worse version of a good match; it is unplayable for a competitive game. Widen skill first, then backfill with bots, then let the player leave. Latency has a hard ceiling; rating does not.
3. Sizing the matcher with arithmetic

Suppose 2,000 players are queued in a mode, matches need 10 players, and arrivals are 40 players per second. A pool with 2,000 candidates produces 200 potential matches instantly if the band is wide enough; at ±50 rating only about 3% of candidates qualify, so the effective pool is 60 players — six matches, roughly 15 seconds of arrivals.

items: Estimate eligible candidates as queue depth × fraction inside the band.
Divide by players per match to get matches available now.
Compare with arrival rate to estimate wait: wait ≈ playersPerMatch / arrivalRate when the pool is empty.
If wait exceeds the mode's tolerance, either widen the band or accept bots/backfill.

blocks.t: For this mode, an empty pool means 10 / 40 = 0.25 s between qualifying arrivals, so waits are dominated by search quality rather than supply — which is why band widening matters more than matcher speed. In a low-population mode at 2 players per second, the same match takes 5 s of arrivals: supply is the problem, and no algorithm fixes it. That is when you backfill.
4. The match function

Two properties matter. Sorting by enqueue time prevents starvation: the oldest ticket always anchors first. And quality is a number, not a boolean, so you can log it and tune thresholds against real data instead of arguing.

blocks.title: Log the counterfactual
blocks.t: For every match, record the quality you accepted and the quality you would have had 10 seconds later. That single metric tells you whether your bands are too tight or too loose, and it is impossible to reconstruct after the fact.
5. Failure modes

head: Symptom
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Pool expansion over time; backfill bots
Track recent opponents, add a diversity term
Players load into a dead lobby
Match accepted but server allocation failed
Reserve capacity before accepting; timeout and requeue
Show estimated wait and an expanding search indicator
Full scan over all tickets every cycle
Index by region and rating; process in bounded batches

blocks.title: Exercise: design a 3v3 mode at low population
blocks.prompt: 3v3, 400 players queued globally, 6 players per match, 15 players/second arriving, players tolerate 45 seconds. Design the pools and expansion, and handle a region with only 40 queued players.
blocks.hint: Compute the wait from arrivals first, then decide whether skill bands or regions must widen.
blocks.solution: Global supply gives 6/15 = 0.4 s per match, so waits are quality-bound, not supply-bound. Use a single pool keyed by mode, band ±75 expanding every 15 s to ±300, region preferred but allow cross-region under 120 ms. For the 40-player region, supply gives one match per 0.4 s only if those players are eligible; with ±75 perhaps 20% qualify, so waits stretch to ~2 s of arrivals — fine. The real risk is a 40-player region at night where 6 simultaneous players may not exist: allow cross-region after 20 s, backfill with bots after 40 s, and never widen ping past 120 ms.

blocks.t: 6. Review checklist

items: Expansion policy is written per mode, with time thresholds.
Latency has a hard ceiling; skill does not.
The match function is pure and returns a quality score.
Queue time, match quality and cancellation rate are all measured.
Server allocation failure has a defined player-visible path.
Bots or backfill exist for low-population modes.

quiz.q: The oldest tickets anchor first in the match function in order to:
quiz.a: Prevent starvation of long-waiting players
quiz.why: Without an age-first anchor, a steady stream of new players can keep matching each other while old tickets wait indefinitely. Fairness has to be explicit.

quiz.q: Which dimension should never be widened to shorten a queue?
quiz.a: Latency beyond the game's playable ceiling
o: Latency beyond the game's playable ceiling
Region grouping within a ping limit
quiz.why: Skill mismatch degrades a match; latency can make it unplayable. Widening skill is a quality decision; widening ping is a correctness decision.

quiz.q: In Open Match, your custom logic belongs in:
quiz.a: The match function
quiz.why: Open Match supplies the frontend, pools, ticket storage and the fetch loop. The match function is the extension point that decides which tickets form a match.

quiz.q: A match is accepted but the game server fails to start. The user-visible requirement is:
quiz.a: A defined timeout and requeue, without losing the player
o: A defined timeout and requeue, without losing the player
quiz.why: Allocation is the most failure-prone step. The player must be returned to the queue with priority, or the match quality work is wasted.

title: Diagrams and Decision Records
subtitle: Draw four levels of detail, then write down why — so the design survives you.
outcomes: Draw context, container, component and sequence views without mixing audiences.
Apply the notation and layout rules that keep a diagram reviewable.
Write an ADR that records the trade-off and the rejected option.
Keep diagrams from drifting away from the running system.

blocks.title: A diagram answers one question
blocks.t: If you cannot say which question a diagram answers, it will answer none. 'Show me the whole system' is not a question; 'what does a checkout request touch?' is.
1. Four levels, four audiences

head: Level
Shows
Audience
Rule
rows: The system as one box, users, external systems
Every arrow is a real network call
Only for the container under discussion

blocks.caption: Container view of a course platform

blocks.t: Notice what the container view omits: no classes, no tables, no library choices. Every box is something you deploy; every arrow is something that can fail at 3 a.m.
2. Notation rules that survive review

left.title: Do
items: One direction per arrow, labelled with the protocol or intent.
Group by trust boundary or deployment boundary, not by colour preference.
Keep boxes axis-aligned; let white space carry grouping.
Split a diagram that needs zooming to read.
Include a legend when you use shapes or colours for meaning.

right.title: Avoid
items: Arrows without labels: is that a call, an event, or a dependency?
Mixing runtime flow and static structure in one picture.
Colour as the only carrier of meaning — inaccessible and unprintable.
A diagram that includes the database but not who may write to it.
Decorative icons that imply technology you do not use.

blocks.title: Stale diagrams are worse than none
blocks.t: A missing diagram makes people ask. A wrong diagram makes them build on a false assumption. If a diagram is not regenerated or reviewed as part of the change, delete it.
3. The ADR
An architecture decision record is one page, immutable once accepted. It exists so that in eight months nobody re-litigates a settled question or silently reverses it.

head: Field
Content
rows: The forces: load, deadline, team size, compliance, existing stack
One sentence, active voice: 'We will cache product pages at the edge for 60 s.'
What else was considered, and the specific reason each lost
What gets easier, what gets harder, what we must now monitor

blocks.t:
# ADR-007: Edge-cache product pages instead of adding read replicas

Status: accepted (2026-03-04)

Context
  Product pages are 78% of read traffic and tolerate seconds of staleness.
  p95 is 340 ms with a single primary; the catalogue table is 40 GB and
  only ~20% of rows are requested in any hour.

Decision
  Cache rendered product pages at the CDN for 60 s, keyed by product id
  and locale, purged on catalogue publish.

Alternatives
  - Read replicas: scales reads but leaves 340 ms origin latency for every
    cache miss and adds failover surface.
  - Application cache: helps, but does not remove the network round trip
    for distant users.

Consequences
  + p95 for cached pages ~40 ms; primary read load drops by an estimated 80%.
  - Up to 60 s of stale price display: price changes must purge immediately.
  - New dependency on the CDN's purge API; alert if purge failures exceed 0.1%.
The value is in the alternatives and consequences. A decision without rejected options is a note, not a record — six months later nobody knows whether the alternative was considered or simply missed.
4. Keeping it true

items: Store diagrams and ADRs next to the code they describe, in the same repository.
Make the diagram part of the pull request for changes that add a component or a call.
Generate what can be generated: service maps from deployment metadata, ER diagrams from migrations.
Review the context diagram once a quarter with the people on call, not with the people who drew it.
Supersede ADRs; never edit history. The chain of decisions is the useful artefact.

blocks.title: Exercise: write the ADR you are avoiding
blocks.prompt: Your team is arguing about whether to split the monolith. Write the ADR in six fields, including what you would have to believe for the split to pay off.
blocks.hint: Consequences should be measurable. 'Better scalability' is not a consequence; 'deploy frequency from weekly to daily' is.
blocks.solution: Context: 14 engineers, weekly release train, one deploy blocking all features, checkout and catalogue sharing a database with lock contention. Decision: keep the monolith, extract the notification worker only, revisit in two quarters. Alternatives: full split (3-5x operational load for a 14-person team, no independent scaling need demonstrated), modular monolith with enforced package boundaries (chosen as the middle path). Consequences: + release train unchanged, contention reduced by moving the worker; - no independent scaling yet; must monitor deploy duration and cross-module coupling, and set a review date. What we would have to believe: that deploy coordination, not infrastructure, is the actual bottleneck — if profiling later shows catalogue load starving checkout, the decision is superseded.

blocks.t: 5. Review checklist

items: Each diagram states its question and audience.
Every arrow is labelled; every box is deployable at container level.
Colour is never the only signal; a legend exists where needed.
ADRs have alternatives and measurable consequences.
Diagrams and ADRs live with the code and are reviewed on change.

quiz.q: A container diagram should show:
quiz.a: Deployable units and the protocols between them
o: Deployable units and the protocols between them
quiz.why: Containers are the deployable/runtime units — apps, services, data stores. Classes belong at code level, tables at data level, and neither helps a runtime discussion.

quiz.q: The most valuable part of an ADR is:
quiz.a: The alternatives and their rejection reasons
o: The alternatives and their rejection reasons
quiz.why: Without the rejected options, the record cannot prevent the same debate recurring, and nobody can tell whether a constraint has since changed.

quiz.q: Why is an unlabelled arrow a defect?
quiz.a: It hides whether it is a synchronous call, an event, or a dependency
o: It hides whether it is a synchronous call, an event, or a dependency
quiz.why: The label carries the failure semantics. A synchronous call can block the caller; an event cannot. The reader cannot review coupling without it.

quiz.q: Which practice keeps documentation honest?
quiz.a: Reviewing diagrams in the pull request that changes the system
o: Reviewing diagrams in the pull request that changes the system
Keeping diagrams in a wiki nobody edits
quiz.why: Drift happens at change time. Making the diagram part of the change review is the only mechanism that keeps it within a commit of reality.

title: Capstone: Design and Defend a Global Live Classroom
subtitle: Requirements, estimates, a design, and the review questions that expose it.
outcomes: Convert a vague product brief into requirements and quality scenarios.
Produce capacity estimates before drawing anything.
Choose a consistency and caching model per data type.
Run a design review against failure, cost and operability.

blocks.t: This is the synthesis exercise. Everything in the library shows up somewhere: requirements, consistency, caching, resilience, data placement, documentation. Work it on paper before reading the model answer.
The brief

Build a live-classroom platform. Instructors run sessions for up to 500 concurrent learners with video, slides, a shared code editor, polls and chat. Sessions are recorded. Learners keep progress and notes forever. The company sells to schools in the EU, India and the US, and each region's data-protection rules must be respected. Target: 1 million monthly active learners, with a Monday 09:00 peak in each region.
Step 1 — Requirements you can test

head: Quality
Scenario
Target
rows: Chat message visible to all participants in a 500-person session
A learner can open a recorded lesson
A submitted assignment is never lost
A learner's own note appears immediately on refresh
EU learner data stays in the EU

blocks.title: Why scenarios beat adjectives
blocks.t: 'Scalable' cannot be reviewed. '500 participants, p95 under 300 ms' can be measured, argued about, and failed honestly.
Step 2 — Estimates before architecture

1M monthly active learners. Monday peak: assume 8% of MAU concurrent at once, across three regions, so about 80,000 concurrent, of which perhaps 60% are in live sessions: 48,000 live participants, in sessions of ~300, so roughly 160 concurrent sessions per peak region.

Two numbers change the design immediately. 72 Gbit/s of video egress makes a CDN mandatory — you cannot serve that from application servers, and the cost target forces aggressive edge caching of recordings. And 9,600 messages/second is trivial for a broker but impossible for a single WebSocket server, so chat needs fan-out and interest management.
Step 3 — Shape of the system

blocks.caption: One region; replicated by data class

blocks.t: The key structural decision: split by data class, not by feature. Video is immutable and cacheable at the edge. Live session state is ephemeral and in memory. Learner records are transactional and must respect residency. Forcing all three through one service is what produces a system that is slow at video and fragile at records.
Step 4 — Decide per data type

blocks.title: Residency is a design constraint, not a deployment setting
blocks.t: If EU PII may not leave the EU, then a global user table, a global search index and a global analytics warehouse are all violations. Group data by residency class first, then design around it.
Step 5 — Where this design fails

items: A session's room owner dies mid-class. Need reconnect + state replay from the last snapshot, and a client that tolerates a visible pause.
Chat fan-out saturates on a 5,000-person keynote. Need sampling or read-only mode above a threshold, and this must be product-approved before the event.
A Monday peak coincides with a CDN regional incident. Need a lower-bitrate fallback and a session-materials-only mode.
Assignment submission retries after a timeout. Need idempotency keys, or students submit twice and see two grades.
A schema change to progress tables during term time. Need expand/contract and a migration window.
Cost blowout from recording egress. Need per-region cost dashboards and a storage tiering policy.

blocks.t: Step 6 — The review questions

items: What is the single point of failure, and what happens in the 30 seconds after it dies?
Which number in the estimate is most likely wrong, and how would you find out cheaply?
What data can be stale, for how long, and who notices?
What happens at 3× peak? What breaks first, and does it break safely?
How do you deploy this on a Monday morning without dropping a live class?
Which part would you delete if the budget were cut in half?

blocks.t: The answer to the last question is the real test of an architecture: if nothing can be removed, the design has no priorities, only wishes.

blocks.title: Capstone deliverable
blocks.prompt: Produce the one-page design: six quality scenarios with numbers, capacity estimates, a container diagram, a consistency/placement table, and your top three risks with mitigations. Then run the six review questions against it.
blocks.hint: Do the estimates before the diagram. Most designs fail because the numbers came after the picture.
blocks.solution: A defensible answer has: (1) at least one hard latency and one durability scenario; (2) peak concurrency derived from MAU rather than guessed, with the multiplication visible; (3) a diagram where every arrow is a network call and every box is deployable; (4) consistency stated per data type, including which reads may be stale; (5) named failure modes with a user-visible behaviour, not just a mitigation; (6) an explicit statement of what you would cut. If your design cannot name what it would cut under budget pressure, it has not made a trade — it has listed everything you want.

quiz.q: Why estimate capacity before drawing the architecture?
quiz.a: The numbers eliminate whole design options early
o: The numbers eliminate whole design options early
quiz.why: 72 Gbit/s of egress settles the CDN question instantly. Without the multiplication, teams draw components they cannot afford and discover it in production.

quiz.q: Which data class should be pinned to a region for residency?
quiz.a: Learner PII such as names and notes
o: Learner PII such as names and notes
quiz.why: Residency constrains personal data. Recordings and public catalogues are not personal; aggregates usually must be de-identified, which is a separate decision.

quiz.q: A 500-person session at 20 Hz chat fan-out is a problem mainly because:
quiz.a: Per-room fan-out multiplies server egress and connection count
o: Per-room fan-out multiplies server egress and connection count
quiz.why: Each message is copied to every participant, so cost grows with participants × messages. That is why interest management, sampling and read-only modes exist.

quiz.q: The strongest sign of a prioritised design is:
quiz.a: A clear answer to what would be removed under budget pressure
o: A clear answer to what would be removed under budget pressure
A large diagram with many services
quiz.why: Architecture is the art of deciding what not to build. A design where nothing can be cut has made no trade-offs, so it cannot be defended under constraint.
